summary: Teach series vs parallel circuits (ages 12–13) by structured CONTRAST of the SAME two bulbs built both ways, tying each rule to meter readings at several points and to a practical consequence. Secure: in series the current is the same everywhere and component voltages add to the supply; in parallel each branch gets the full supply voltage and branch currents add where they meet. Foreground the counter-intuitive result that adding a parallel branch LOWERS total resistance and RAISES total current — the opposite of adding a series component. Use predict-then-test relentlessly (add/remove a bulb, watch brightness and meters) and anchor 'why homes are wired in parallel' in observable consequences. A recomputing circuit simulation (or a hands-on physical build) is the central activity; a comparison quiz, an annotated diagram-pair reference, and an electrician design dialogue are complementary. This is a UK KS3-anchored topic (parallel first met here after KS2 series-only); no middle-school NGSS PE covers series/parallel DC-circuit analysis.
misconceptions: Mixing up which quantity is shared vs added — e.g. thinking voltage is the same everywhere in series, or that current splits but voltage adds in parallel; the rules are crossed between the two configurations.
Believing current splits EQUALLY at a parallel junction regardless of the branches — it divides according to resistance, with more current through the lower-resistance branch.
Thinking adding a parallel branch reduces the total current — it INCREASES it (lower total resistance, more routes for charge).
Expecting parallel bulbs to be dimmer than a single bulb — each branch gets the full supply voltage, so each is as bright as a lone bulb (unlike series, where they share and dim).
The current-used-up error resurfacing in series — thinking the bulb nearest the battery is brighter; in series the current is the same everywhere and identical bulbs are equally bright.
Assuming more components always means more total resistance — true in series, FALSE in parallel, where adding branches LOWERS the total resistance.
Thinking household circuits are series — they are parallel, so each appliance gets full voltage and works independently.

activities.title: Build it both ways: series and parallel on the same two bulbs
steps: Start with one bulb lit from a cell; note its brightness as a baseline.
Add a SECOND bulb IN SERIES; before testing, predict what happens to the first bulb's brightness, then observe (both dim together) and watch the ammeter reading fall.
Reconfigure the same two bulbs into PARALLEL; predict first, then observe the first bulb stays at full brightness (ideal cell) while the main-line current rises.
Place an ammeter at several points: in series confirm all readings are equal; in parallel confirm the branch currents add to the main-line current where branches meet.
Place a voltmeter across components: in series confirm the component voltages add to the supply; in parallel confirm each branch reads the full supply voltage.
Do the unscrew/remove test: remove one bulb in series (whole circuit goes dark) and in parallel (the other stays lit); trace the loop for the remaining parallel bulb to see it is still complete.
If a total-resistance readout is available, compare it as you add a series component (resistance up, current down) vs a parallel branch (resistance down, current up).
Try a household mode wiring appliances across the full supply in parallel, switching each independently.
activities.insight: Series and parallel obey crossed rules: series shares the voltage (bulbs dimmer, current same everywhere, one break kills all) while parallel gives each branch the full voltage on its own loop (full brightness with an ideal cell, currents add, independent switching). Adding a parallel branch opens more routes for charge, so total resistance drops and total current rises. Houses are wired in parallel because each device gets the full supply voltage and can be switched, or can fail, independently.

activities.title: Sort and predict: series vs parallel rules
steps: Sort statements into SERIES vs PARALLEL columns: 'current same everywhere', 'voltages across components add to the supply', 'each branch gets the full supply voltage', 'branch currents add where they meet'.
Predict the brightness of the first bulb when a second bulb is added in series, then when added in parallel.
Answer 'why is household wiring parallel?' and justify by a consequence (full voltage to each device, independent switching, one failing leaves others working).
Predict what happens to the total current when a parallel branch is added.
Rank circuits by total resistance as series components are added vs as parallel branches are added.
activities.insight: The rules and their practical consequences can be stated precisely and matched to the correct configuration, consolidating the contrast learned by building.

activities.title: Reference diagram pair: the rules at a glance
steps: Study a labelled pair of diagrams of the SAME components in series and in parallel, with meters placed at multiple points.
On the series diagram, note 'current same everywhere / component voltages add to supply'; on the parallel diagram, note 'each branch full supply voltage / branch currents add at the junction'.
Reveal the 'unscrew one' outcome for each: series goes dark, parallel keeps the rest lit.
Use the junction close-up to see branch currents adding where they meet.
activities.insight: A compact reference ties the crossed rules and the household-wiring case to clear diagrams, supporting recall after the active work.

activities.title: Electrician's design problem: series or parallel?
steps: Take on real design problems with an electrician persona: how to wire old-style fairy lights vs a house lighting circuit.

Argue, for each case, whether series or parallel is appropriate and give the consequence-based reason (does one failing kill the rest? does each device get full voltage? can each be switched independently?).
Explain why a house is NOT wired in series by describing what would go wrong if one lamp failed.
Contrast old series fairy-lights (one blows, all go out) with parallel wiring.
activities.insight: Choosing a configuration for a real purpose forces the learner to reason from the rules to consequences, reinforcing why parallel is standard for independent, full-brightness, fault-tolerant devices.

checkQuestion: You have two identical bulbs. In circuit A they're in series; in circuit B they're in parallel, both on the same battery. Compare how bright the bulbs are in A versus B, and explain what happens to EACH bulb if you unscrew one of the two.
checkAnswer: In series the two bulbs share the battery's voltage, so each is dimmer than a single bulb; and because it's one loop, unscrewing either one breaks the loop and BOTH go out. In parallel each bulb gets the full battery voltage across its own branch, so each is as bright as a single bulb and the branches are independent — unscrew one and the other stays lit. That full voltage and independence is why household wiring is parallel.
